scenes.narration: The feeling that The House of the Seven Gables (film) means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. The House of the Seven Gables is a 1940 Gothic drama film based on the 1851 novel of the same name by Nathaniel Hawthorne. It stars George Sanders, Margaret Lindsay, and Vincent Price, and tells the story of a family consumed by greed in which one brother frames another for murder.

Nothing in The House of the Seven Gables (film) was built for you — it was built for reproduction. It is a remake of the 1910 film of the same name, which starred Mary Fuller. The film's musical score was nominated for the Oscar for Best Original Score.

The psychology underneath The House of the Seven Gables (film) is simpler and older than the story on top. The plot of the film differs dramatically from that of Hawthorne's novel. Colonel Jaffrey Pyncheon falsely accused a poor carpenter, Matthew Maule, of witchcraft during the Salem witch trials.

Behind The House of the Seven Gables (film) sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Pyncheon took his land and built the luxurious Pyncheon home on it. The family has lived during the next 160 years desperately afraid of the "Maule curse".

The nihilist does not deny The House of the Seven Gables (film) — he only refuses to flatter it. Pyncheon's great-great-grandson Jaffrey Pyncheon (George Sanders) is a lawyer just embarking on his career. His elder brother, Clifford (Vincent Price), lives at home with their father, Gerald Pyncheon (Gilbert Emery).

What culture calls destiny in The House of the Seven Gables (film) is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Jaffrey is obsessed with legends that say a vast sum of money is hidden in the Pyncheon house. Jaffrey is summoned to his father's home when Clifford informs him that the house is to be sold to pay his father's debts.

The genes do not care about The House of the Seven Gables (film); they care about copies. Jaffrey, terrified at losing the lost treasure, pries up floorboards and searches in the walls at night for the lost gold. He wants to marry his cousin, Hepzibah Pyncheon (Margaret Lindsay), sell the house, and move to New York City.

Take away the meaning and The House of the Seven Gables (film) still functions — that is the disturbing part. When Gerald decides not to sell the house after all, Clifford and his father argue violently. Gerald dies of a heart attack, and strikes his head as he falls.

The unconscious does not argue with The House of the Seven Gables (film); it simply acts first. Clifford is convicted and imprisoned, but renews "Maule's curse" upon Jaffrey before being led away. Gerald's will gives all three children sizeable yearly incomes, but leaves the house to Hepzibah.

The House of the Seven Gables (film) feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Hepzibah throws Jaffrey out of the house and seals all the doors and windows so that no light can be admitted. In 1841, Clifford is given a new cellmate, who identifies himself as Matthew Maule (Dick Foran).

The bleak reading of The House of the Seven Gables (film) is also the most testable one. Maule is shortly released, and takes the name "Holgrave." An abolitionist, he rents a room from Hepzibah Pyncheon. Shortly thereafter, a distant cousin dies and Hepzibah takes in the cousin's daughter, Phoebe Pyncheon (Nan Grey).

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about The House of the Seven Gables (film). Desperate for money, Hepzibah opens a small shop in a room of her home. With the beautiful, vivacious Phoebe running the shop, it is a success and earns her much money.

The self that experiences The House of the Seven Gables (film) is a committee, not a king. Jaffrey has invested money from wealthy abolitionists in risky investments involving the slave trade. Realizing he might be able to seize control of the house, Jaffrey uses these rumors to accuse Clifford of insanity.

Reproduction explains more of The House of the Seven Gables (film) than any philosophy dares to admit. Jaffrey visits the house, and hears banging – which he assumes is Clifford searching for the gold. Hepzibah discovers that Holgrave is making these noises, and evicts him from the house despite the protests of Phoebe (who is in love with him).

Once you see The House of the Seven Gables (film) as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. A worried Hepzibah then searches Holgrave's room and discovers he is really Matthew Maule. She warns Clifford, who admits that he has known all along who Holgrave is and that Holgrave is part of his plan to clear his name.

The story The House of the Seven Gables (film) tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Jaffrey visits the house and tells Clifford that he intends to have him committed. Clifford responds by asking Jaffrey to sign a document that clears Clifford's name.

Meaning is not found in The House of the Seven Gables (film) — it is manufactured for it. Deacon Arnold Foster (Miles Mander), who loaned Jaffrey the investment funds, arrives and demands the money back. Panicking, Jaffrey signs the document and tells Clifford that he can have the lost treasure so long as Clifford does not accuse him of murder.

The cold light on The House of the Seven Gables (film) leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. The House of the Seven Gables was first filmed by Edison Studios in 1910. Republic Pictures announced a remake in 1935, but it went into development hell and was never made.

The House of the Seven Gables (film) did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Universal Studios began planning its remake of The House of the Seven Gables probably in early 1939. Pre-production for the film was secretive, as the studio feared that other companies with more financial resources might rush a House of Seven Gables into production before Universal could finish its version.

The honest version of The House of the Seven Gables (film) starts by giving up the comforting part. The studio wanted the picture to be a low-budget B film, which would be released as a double feature with another B film. It was budgeted at a low $152,625 ($3,532,648 in 2025 dollars), but was still considered one of Universal's "prestige" horror films.

Strip The House of the Seven Gables (film) of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Screenwriter Lester Cole says it was unclear why Universal chose to make the film, although it may have been because the book was in the public domain. Smith, however, argues for an economic reason: Horror films were popular again.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — The House of the Seven Gables (film) shows exactly where that breaks. A national outcry against the gruesomeness of the 1935 film The Raven had convinced Universal Studios executives to place a ban on the production of horror films at the studio. But a New York City movie theater ran a triple-bill of Dracula, Frankenstein, and Son of Kong in 1938, and ticket sales were so strong that the theater ran the films 21 hours a day.

What looks like free choice in The House of the Seven Gables (film) is older than choice itself. Universal announced it would begin work on The House of the Seven Gables on October 10, 1939. The studio assigned one of its B-picture producers, Burt Kelly, to oversee the production.

Nobody designed the part of The House of the Seven Gables (film) you experience — it was inherited. Kelly had an extensive background in theater, and had held a number of associate producer and producer positions at various studios. Universal also assigned one of its young staff writers, Harold Greene, to produce a treatment of the novel.

Every serious account of The House of the Seven Gables (film) eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Kelly had his choice of whom to hire as screenwriter, however, and he chose Lester Cole. Kelly had worked with Cole on a number of films, and film historian Bob Herzberg suggests that Kelly held progressive views which were shared by Cole (who openly held communist political views).

Nihilism is not the conclusion of The House of the Seven Gables (film) — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Kelly, who Cole felt had "a real feeling for film and decent human instincts", was also a loyal friend of Cole's. Universal Studios initially balked at Kelly's decision because Cole's salary was $600 a week ($13,888 in 2025 dollars), but Kelly insisted and the studio gave in.

The selfish-gene reading of The House of the Seven Gables (film) makes it less romantic and far more precise. The lengthy novel by Nathaniel Hawthorne needed extensive cutting to turn it into a filmable script. Cole substantially cut much of the beginning of the novel, and altered a good deal of the plot—remaining faithful to the spirit of the novel if not its actual narrative.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. He turned the character of Matthew Maule/"Holgrave" into an abolitionist, and depicted capitalists like Jaffrey Pyncheon and Arnold Foster as illegal slave-traders. He also greatly sharpened Hawthorne's critique of materialism, and depicted the punishment for greed coming not from God (as Hawthorne did) but from moral and freedom-loving people.

Film historian Lawrence Raw has argued that Cole, and to a lesser extent Greene, also wanted the story to attack authoritarianism. Cole in particular was deeply aware of the wave of fascism and dictatorship sweeping across Europe in the 1930s, and Raw argues that Cole transformed the film into a "propaganda piece" in which Jaffrey Pyncheon was a metaphor for governmental tyranny.
